source.title_on_document: An empirical investigation of the impact of ChatGPT on creativity

paper_design_summary: Six online experiments (labelled 1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4, 5) with US MTurk or Prolific participants. Participants were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 website) or Google Web search (Experiments 1, 2A, 3, 4, 5) or no external aid (Human-only, Experiments 2A and 2B) while generating a creative idea for an everyday product problem (toy from given items, repurposing household items, dining table, gift for a teenage girl); Experiments 4 and 5 cross the technology factor with task constraints or empathy framing. Ideas were rated by separate panels of lay judges (six-item originality plus appropriateness creativity score) and, as a robustness check, by three expert judges; Experiment 2B also compares 100 unedited ChatGPT outputs (no people) with human ideas.

eligibility.reason: All six experiments randomly assign individuals to ChatGPT versus Web search and/or no aid (Reporting Summary: randomized via Qualtrics). Each analyzes 194-400 people, well above 50. The outcome is a judge-rated creativity score of each participant's idea. Experiment 2B also includes an ai_vs_human comparison (100 unedited ChatGPT outputs vs human ideas) that is context only.

one_line_finding: Across six online experiments, ideas produced with ChatGPT were rated more creative than ideas produced with Web search (d = 0.32 to 1.01) or with no aid (d = 0.56 in Experiment 2A, 1.88 in Experiment 2B) by lay judges (Table 1, PDF p. 5).
open_questions: Per-arm ns are not printed for any experiment; arm-level counts would need the OSF data (https://osf.io/rzn87/).

Experiment 2B t-tests use df = 297 from a three-group model that pools 200 people with 100 ChatGPT-only outputs; the ChatGPT-assisted vs Human-only contrast's standard error therefore uses a pooled variance that includes AI outputs.
Whether Experiments 1 and 3 were preregistered is not stated; the Reporting Summary lists preregistration only for 2A, 2B, 4 and 5.
Supplementary Notes E (sub-dimensions), F (top-ranked ideas), G (expert ratings, articulateness, verbosity, newness type) and H are not in this PDF and may hold further outcomes.
notes: PDF has 12 pages: article pages 1-9 (journal pp. 1906-1914) and Reporting Summary pages 10-12. Locators give PDF page and journal page. Not listed as outcomes: Experiment 3 self-reported 'idea exposition aid' (ChatGPT 5.16, s.d. 1.96 vs Web search 2.94, s.d. 1.59; t192 = 8.69; d = 1.25; PDF p. 3-4), which is self-report, and other Experiment 3 exploratory self-reports and PANAS (Supplementary Note I); the Experiment 2B correlation of self-reported modification with creativity (r = 0.11, P = 0.291); the pilot surveys (n = 100) in Supplementary Notes A-B. Experiment 2B 'ChatGPT-only' arm has no people and is coded as question 'none' (ai_vs_human). Inconsistencies in the document: (1) Table 1, Experiment 4, the fourth row (mean 4.40, s.d. 0.61) is labelled 'ChatGPT-assisted x Low constraints' but the text gives it as Web-search-assisted; (2) Experiment 2B ChatGPT-only s.d. is 0.40 in Table 1 and the first text mention but 0.30 in the ChatGPT-assisted vs ChatGPT-only sentence (PDF p. 3); (3) the Reporting Summary says the a priori power analysis was for Experiment 2A, while Methods places it in Experiment 2B and the Reporting Summary also says 2A used no statistical method to set sample size; (4) Experiment 2B Methods says participants were randomly assigned to 'one of two conditions' while Results calls it a three-level between-participants design (the third level is AI-only output); (5) the Experiment 3 judges' demographics (mean age 43.11, 50% female) are identical to the Experiment 3 participants'; (6) Experiment 4 Results says participants 'were assigned' and Methods says 'randomly assigned'. Lay-judge creativity is the paper's main outcome; expert ratings are called a robustness check, so lay ratings are coded paper_primary.
